title: Double the fastest machine
hook: A line of four machines makes parts. What does one much faster machine buy you?

knows: a faster machine makes more parts
doesNotKnow: that a line's output is capped by its slowest step, so speeding up any other step changes nothing except the pile in front of the slow one

misconception: Doubling the speed of any station raises the line's output.
objective: The learner can explain that a serial line runs at the pace of its slowest station: doubling station 1 from 12 to 24 parts an hour leaves output at 5, only upgrading the bottleneck raises it, and once it is fast enough the bottleneck moves to the next-slowest station.

claims.text: The Goal builds its story on this: find the constraint (bottleneck), improve it, then look for the next one; improving a non-constraint does not raise the system's output.
claims.source: Goldratt & Cox, The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement (North River Press, 1984), work goldratt-the-goal-1984, the scout-hike (Herbie) chapters, around ch. 13-14 (unconfirmed). The book argues this; the claim is about the book, not the world. Paraphrased in our own words; no quote. Brief: company/domains/briefs/books.md #1.

claims.text: Does it hold up? On a steady line, yes: a serial line's throughput in steady state equals its slowest station's capacity (standard operations maths).
claims.source: Hopp & Spearman, Factory Physics, 3rd ed. (2008), ch. 7 'Basic Factory Dynamics' (bottleneck rate; chapter to confirm). Also checkable by derivation: in a serial line no station can pass on more than it receives, so output = min(rates).

claims.text: For whole firms, the evidence that applying the Theory of Constraints raises performance is mostly case reports.
claims.source: Mabin & Balderstone (2003), 'The performance of the theory of constraints methodology: analysis and discussion of successful TOC applications', International Journal of Operations & Production Management 23(6) (a review of published TOC applications; to confirm). Brief claim 4.

claims.text: Model on the card (chip 'Our model line · piles after 1 hour' and the question): four stations in a row at 12, 9, 5 and 10 parts an hour, station 1 has unlimited raw material, each tap adds 2 parts an hour with 3 upgrades to spend; the pile in front of a station is how many parts wait there after one hour.
claims.source: Lesson model, Demo.tsx: output = min(rates); inflow to station i = min of the rates before it; pile = max(0, inflow - rate) after one hour. The rates are the brief's (company/domains/briefs/books.md #1), not data from the book.

claims.text: Doubling station 1 from 12 to 24 leaves output at 5 an hour (the pile in front of station 2 grows from 3 to 15); three upgrades on station 3 take it to 11, output rises to 9 and the slowest station becomes station 2.
claims.source: min(12, 9, 5, 10) = 5 and min(24, 9, 5, 10) = 5; piles [0, 3, 4, 0] and [0, 15, 4, 0]; min(12, 9, 11, 10) = 9 with station 2 unique slowest. Builder node run 2026-10-14; brief check node company/domains/briefs/checks/books-cycle1-check.mjs.

claims.text: A café takes 40 orders an hour, makes 15 coffees an hour and rings up 30 an hour; a second cashier (60 an hour) still leaves 15 coffees an hour, because the coffee station is the slowest step.
claims.source: min(40, 15, 60) = 15; same rule as c2. Recall item, stipulated example.

recall.question: A café takes 40 orders an hour, makes 15 coffees an hour and rings up 30 an hour. You hire a second cashier, so the till does 60. How many customers get a coffee each hour?
recall.why: The coffee station is the slowest step at 15 an hour, so the café serves 15 whatever the till does; the extra till speed only means more waiting at the coffee machine.
